We’re aligned now:
- **argv arrays** only (no command strings, no `_` mangling)
- optional fields for `cwd/env/stdin/stdout/stderr/capture/timeout` etc.

**HV comment:** This is *the* core primitive for WU deployment to agent chats and for shellboss routing. This is the right foundation.

---

## ✅ DIF-SHELL-PRIMITIVES-POLICY
You’re upping the bar (good):
- define primitives
- ban term-kill patterns
- require tool/version inventory for any command invoked anywhere

**HV comment:** this is a dependency system problem; keep the “policy family” unified so CI can enforce.

---

## ✅ DIF-KINDS-ARE-GENERATED
Your ask: “can we just generate all of these?” → **Yes, CBA.**  
We reserve paths now, but explicitly label machgen as **planned** (not assumed to exist).

**HV comment:** Make the generator live under `library/` and constrain its language footprint to **sh+py+go+rust**. Anything else is an explicit exception with a contract.

---

## ✅ DIF-HIERA (FIRST-CLASS TOOL) + HOME PRIVACY GATE
Big point: **home/.hee must never be implicitly included**. It needs an explicit “this home is allowed” hee-obj manifest (phiera vibes).

**HV comment:** Correct. This prevents “newer in home overrides repo” footguns and supports private/WIP enforcement. This is a **hiera-lookup WU**, not “now.”

Also: keep **system/local/hee** always mentioned as planned tier, even if unused right now.

---

## ✅ DIF-CONTRACT-STACK (GCIC + DRIC family)
You want `contracts_yaml_authority` to include adoption of:
- **GCIC** (top-level contract)
- **DRIC-v1** (GPT-related contract family; name must change because not design→relay only)
- **DRIC-v1-subN** delegates (plug-in model, avoid updating monolithic stack)

**HV comment:** This is the right architecture: stable top-level contract(s) + “subcontracts” to extend without rewriting the root stack.

**Action needed (likely):** `rg` scan to locate gcic/dric artifacts and current locations (md today) to plan formal adoption into YAML hee-obj.

---

## ✅ DIF-MD-EXCEPTIONS + WAIVERS SYSTEM
You already have `waivers.txt` infrastructure (you proved it with `find`). So for `gpt-prompting-guide.md` we choose:

- **Option A:** adopt the existing waiver system explicitly as the MD-exception mechanism
- **Option B:** replace it later, but **retrofit** the existing waivers to avoid breaking governance

**HV comment:** CBA is **adopt** (A) first; replacement (B) is a later WU with migration plan.

---

## ✅ DIF-PATH-NOTATION `{repo}/...`
You want `{repo}/…` as **documentation notation**, not a placeholder in code, and placeholders are only allowed when they do work (Jinja) and are explicitly waived.

**HV comment:** agree. Mark it as “notation-only” in docs and forbid in code unless under Jinja contract.

---

## ✅ DIF-SQZ-ROLL DISCOVERY (needs rg/find)
You said sqz-roll policy files already exist on main. So we need an `rg/find` task to locate:
- existing sqz-roll(s)
- existing naming patterns and policy

**HV comment:** yes. Don’t invent. Discover and merge.

---

## ✅ DIF-LIBRARY RULES (structure + shellboss config)
You want:
- `library/` has core language dirs/modules for **sh+py+go+rust**
- non-core tools (machgen) can exist, but must be declared
- shellboss needs a clear config file describing capabilities, including itself

**HV comment:** correct. This also supports “shellboss is the only runner.”

---

## ✅ DIF-KEYS numbering + padding/toggle
You want:
- numbered DIF keys, pad 4 now
- ability to change padding later (toggle)
- fear: if we use all 4 digits, we “failed” to build the better system

**HV comment:** I like the “toggleable padding” part, but the “using all 4 digits = failure” is a cute cultural guardrail, not an operational truth. Still worth encoding as a *warning* rule, not a hard fail.

Proposed shape:
- `dif_id: DIF-0001-TS-NAME`
- `dif_pad: 4` (policy-controlled)

```yaml
apiVersion: hee/v1
kind: Pill
metadata:
  name: proposed-filepaths-2026-02-10_1900
  description: Proposed filepaths (YAML-first) for settled DIF items; includes hiera-lookup caveats; no content emitted yet.
spec:
  identity:
    user: spencer
    gh_user: spencerbutler
  scope:
    repo: human-execution-engine
    includes_planned_tier: system/local/hee
  hiera:
    precedence_high_to_low:
      - system/local/hee
      - home/.hee
      - repo/.hee
      - repo/hee
      - repo/contracts
      - repo/schemas
    conflicts:
      status: TBD
      note: conflict resolution and home/.hee inclusion policy are a first-class hiera-lookup task (phiera-style).
    home_inclusion:
      status: TBD
      note: home/.hee must not be implicitly included; requires an explicit hee-obj allowlist/manifest per-home to avoid private/WIP leakage and lock-in.
  path_notation:
    style: "{repo}/path"
    note: notation only (documentation); placeholders must not appear in code unless they do work; placeholder use is an explicit exception policy item.
  paths:
    contracts_yaml_authority:
      - "{repo}/contracts/file-writing.policy.v1.yaml"
      - "{repo}/contracts/mdshell.policy.v1.yaml"
      - "{repo}/contracts/hiera.lookup.policy.v1.yaml"
      - "{repo}/contracts/identity.policy.v1.yaml"
      - "{repo}/contracts/depends.registry.policy.v1.yaml"
      - "{repo}/contracts/pn.policy.v1.yaml"
      - "{repo}/contracts/kind.registry.v1.yaml"
      - "{repo}/contracts/validate.policy.v1.yaml"
      - "{repo}/contracts/jinja.render.policy.v1.yaml"
    cards_yaml_authority:
      - "{repo}/hee/cards/mets.card.v1.yaml"
      - "{repo}/hee/cards/rg-scan.card.v1.yaml"
      - "{repo}/hee/cards/shellboss.card.v1.yaml"
      - "{repo}/hee/cards/notes-capture-prompts.card.v1.yaml"
      - "{repo}/hee/cards/leg1-ideas-to-canon.card.v1.yaml"
      - "{repo}/hee/cards/hee-words.dictionary.card.v1.yaml"
      - "{repo}/hee/cards/hee-words.thesaurus.card.v1.yaml"
      - "{repo}/hee/cards/dif.style-and-usage.card.v1.yaml"
    pills_yaml_authority:
      - "{repo}/hee/pills/q-sqz-roll-2026-02-10_1851.pill.v1.yaml"
    md_exceptions_allowed:
      - "{repo}/hee/cards/gpt-prompting-guide.md"
    generated_outputs:
      - "{repo}/generated/"
      - "{repo}/generated/hee/cards/"
      - "{repo}/generated/hee/pills/"
    machgen:
      status: planned
      note: machgen is not assumed to exist yet; paths are reserved for future library-owned implementation.
      library_machgen_and_tools:
        - "{repo}/library/machgen/"
        - "{repo}/library/machgen/kind-registry/"
        - "{repo}/library/machgen/jinja-render/"
        - "{repo}/library/validate/"

Here’s the **single-focus dif list** I think we should commit to (and what I’m taking as the reconciled direction). I’m keeping each item “one knob.”

## Single-focus DIFs

### DIF-TS-NAME
**Decision:** session roll names use `YYYY-MM-DD_HHMM` (24h)  
Example: `q-sqz-roll-2026-02-10_1851` ✅

### DIF-OPER-ID
**Decision:** don’t store absolute home paths; store an oper identity K:V that can be resolved.  
Proposed canonical form:
- `oper: "${HOME}:${GH_REPO_USER}"` (resolved at runtime by shellboss)
- optionally store `oper_home_ref: "$HOME"` and `oper_repo_user_ref: "$GH_REPO_USER"` if we need explicitness later.

### DIF-YAML-ONE-KV-PER-LINE
**Decision:** YAML authoring rule is **“one k:v per line”** (no double pairs).  
Clarification: `::` as a token is fine; it’s the **two k:v pairs on one line** we ban. (minor)

### DIF-CMD-ENCODING
**Decision:** **never** do `_` space-mangling for commands.  
Canonical command representation is:
- `argv: [...]` arrays (no command strings)
- optional separate fields for `cwd`, `env`, `stdin`, `stdout`, `stderr`, `capture`, `timeout`, etc.

This becomes the core WU→agent-chat deployment mechanism.

### DIF-SHELL-PRIMITIVES-POLICY
**Decision:** define “POSIX sh primitives” + ban term-kill patterns under a single policy family; and require tool/version documentation for any command invoked anywhere in-repo.

This ties into dependency inventory: versions, min/max, RTFM refs.

### DIF-KINDS-ARE-GENERATED
**Decision:** Kind registry + foundational decls are **generated** (CBA now), via a simple workflow (Makefile or equivalent) living in `library/`.  
shellboss handles runtime invocation; CI enforces correctness.

### DIF-PN-FLEX-METS
**Decision:** pN system is flexible + MET-driven; definitions live as schema/policy, not hardcoded prose. (We’ll design in the WU.)

### DIF-PREFLIGHT-MDSHELL
**Decision:** before emitting any mdshell heredocs, run a **tiny preflight mdshell** that:
- confirms repo dir + branch
- confirms expected dirs/files existence
- anchored to SOA
- emits **one** k:v evidence line
- uses circle r/g/y + b/lb indicators (info-only / inert)
- defines expected result before doing anything

### DIF-VALIDATION-RUNNER
**Decision:** schema validation is `argv` arrays + **shellboss is the only runner** contract.  
Your corrected example is the canon:
- `validate_argv: ["shellboss","jsonschema_validate","--schema","schemas/hee/v1/hee-object.schema.json","--in","-"]`

---

- adjust tiers to `repo/contracts` etc.
- add `oper` identity convention
- add “one k:v per line” rule
- add preflight mdshell requirement
- shift kinds registry to “generated via library + shellboss”

That said, **CBA here** (given your constraints) is:

## CBA decision
### ✅ Best HV path
**Canonical entrypoint = shellboss**, and shellboss runs a **deterministic validator** in **POSIX sh primitives**.

Why:
- You already have a stable, hashed path: `/home/spencer/.local/bin/shellboss`
- You already want “all mdshell pasteables go through shellboss”
- It avoids per-repo tool drift (“does this machine have node/ajv?”)

So: **don’t pick “ajv vs python vs node” as a human habit**. Pick **shellboss** as the habit, and shellboss chooses the validator.

## What to do now (practical “path to best HV option”)
### Phase 0 (now): minimal validation command line
In hee-obj YAML, store something like:

- `validate_cmd_argv`: an argv array (no space-mangling)
- `validate_via`: `shellboss`

Example shape (not emitting files yet):
- `validate_via: shellboss`
- `validate_argv: ["shellboss","jsonschema_validate","--schema","schemas/hee/v1/hee-object.schema.json","--in","-"]`

### Phase 1: implement shellboss validator subcommand
Shellboss gets a subcommand that:
- accepts YAML input (stdin or file)
- converts YAML → JSON deterministically (tool choice internal)
- validates JSON against schema
- exits non-zero on fail
- prints concise errors

### Phase 2: `hee validate` becomes a thin wrapper
Later, `hee validate` just delegates to shellboss (or reuses the same library code), but **the contract stays “go through shellboss.”**

## What’s AJV’s role in this plan?
AJV is just **one possible engine** shellboss can use *internally* if/when Node is acceptable. But you don’t bake Node dependency into every workflow right now.

## DIF notes

### 1) **hee-object compliance + schema validation**
- You want “self-validating is vhee”: that implies a **standard validation command** is part of every hee-obj (or at least every pill/card that claims compliance).
- ⚠️ We need to decide **mechanism**: `ajv` vs `python` vs `node` wrapper vs `hee` binary.
  - My vote: **one canonical tool entrypoint** (eventually `hee validate ...`) but in the meantime include a **POSIX sh primitive** command that uses whatever tool is already in repo/toolchain.
- DIF to capture in policy: **validation commands should be stored with `_` terse** args.

### 2) **Time / naming**
- You want `name: q-sqz-roll-20260210` replaced with something human readable + `HHHH_MM`.
  - DIF: define exact format now so we don’t drift. Example: `q-sqz-roll-2026-02-10_1851` (24h), or `..._18_51` (if you want underscore-separated).
- Also: add `hee_epoch` as authoritative, and `ts_human` derived. You already gave the pattern.

### 3) **Identity fields**
- Need `oper:` and `oper_repo_user:` (or similar) to ground `$HOME` and `gh/<repo-user>`.
  - DIF: decide if `oper_home:` is a **path** or a **symbol**. (I’d avoid absolute paths in canon; store a key like `oper_home_ref: "$HOME"` and let shellboss resolve.)

### 4) **Hiera tiers specificity**
- Change `contracts/` → `repo/contracts/` (and likely `repo/hee/`, `repo/.hee/` etc.).
- DIF: decide whether the tier list is **resolution order** vs **inventory**. If order, name it `precedence_high_to_low` explicitly.

### 5) **YAML style rules**
You added several **very enforceable** constraints; we should group them under a single policy object (file-writing policy):

- **English contractions banned** (applies to YAML and Markdown authoring rules, governed by Jinja2 contract).
- **Never write YAML with `::` on the same line unless quoted**.
- **Prefer terse keys/values when readability preserved**.
- **Commands/args should be documented in `_` form** to reduce copy/paste risk.
- DIF: define “reasonable exception” once (and reuse) so it’s not vibes.

### 6) **The `text:` example with shell quoting**
This line is a perfect example of why the `_` command policy matters:

```yaml
text: 'output="$(bash ci/governance/check.sh --path governance/fixtures/ok-minimal 2>&1)"'
```

- DIF: if we standardize “machine-gen tools should `s/ /_/g` for exact commands,” we must define **how to rehydrate** safely back to real shell. Otherwise we’ll create a new footgun.
- Suggestion: store commands in a structured form instead:
  - `argv: ["bash","ci/governance/check.sh","--path","governance/fixtures/ok-minimal"]`
  - and separately store `redir: "2>&1"` or `capture: true`
- That’s *much* safer than space-mangling.

### 7) **Shell and mdshell mandates**
These are foundational and should be in the same policy group:

- Shell functions: `_` separator, **min 2 words**
- Shell scripts with >1 word: **`-` only**
- All mdshell pasteables: **POSIX sh primitives**
- Future: all mdshell goes through **shellboss full stop**
- DIF: we should define “primitive” and explicitly ban “term-kill patterns” you already care about (exits/traps/unbalanced quotes etc.) in that same policy family.

### 8) **Kind registry + top-level declarations**
- This is a dependency for real hee-obj compliance: we need a **kind registry** (allowed kinds, versioning, directory mapping).
- DIF: decide “where kinds live” (repo path) and how enforcement happens (CI step vs `hee validate`).

### 9) **Everything gets pN anchored to WU**
- Great. DIF: define:
  - what `p0..pN` means (time-to-fix, blast radius, blocking)
  - anchoring format: `wu: tmux-ux` + `step: 03` etc.
- Also capture the CI migration nuance:
  - “CI will eventually migrate into `library/`” (tools, not `ci/` folder) as `p3`.

   - contractions ban

   - MD exception dif rules

      tiers_intended:
        - system/local/hee
        - home/.hee
        - repo/.hee
        - repo/hee
        - contracts/
  decisions:
    git_history:
      heuristics:
        preserve_commits_default_if:
          - meaningful
          - separable
          - happy_to_revert_cherrypick_bisect_individually
        preserve_commits_pays_off_only_if: commit_quality_is_maintained (ideally each commit compiles/tests or is clearly-scoped structural moves)
      mets_note: squash_rate_as_fatigue_signal_requires_context (avoid false positives for mechanical squashes)
  queue:
    cards_prepared_not_emitted:
      - id: helpful-tips.gh-and-shell
        intent: card(s) with helpful tips from this session (held until emit).
        includes:
          - gh_pr_edit_body_newlines:
              - heredoc_body_file_stdin
              - ansi_c_quoting_body
              - editor_body
          - jq_filter_strings_need_quotes_for_state_success
          - gh_rules_required_check_name_mismatch_fix (file-path-required-check vs actual check name)
      - id: mets
        intent: dedicated MET card (what we know, what we suggest).
        includes:
          - merge_strategy (squash|merge|rebase)
          - commit_quality_tag (separable|dependent|noisy)
          - green_commit_ratio
          - reason_squash (mechanical|policy|churn|fatigue|unknown)
          - ci_rerun_count
          - time_to_green
      - id: rg-scan
        intent: rg scan triage patterns + evidence capture.
        evidence:
          cmd: "rg ' governance/' .github/ ci/ .pre-commit-config.yaml"
          hits:
            - file: .github/workflows/governance.yaml
              line: 84
              text: 'output="$(bash ci/governance/check.sh --path governance/fixtures/ok-minimal 2>&1)"'
            - file: .github/workflows/governance.yaml
              line: 122
              text: 'output="$(bash ci/governance/check.sh --path governance/fixtures/bad-missing-doctrine-doc 2>&1)"'
      - id: shellboss
        intent: shellboss card additions (branch prompt extraction).
        needs_definition: true
        branch_prompt_snippets:
          preferred_modern_git: "printf '(%s) ' \"$(git branch --show-current 2>/dev/null)\""
          fallback_old_git: "printf '(%s) ' \"$(git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD 2>/dev/null)\""
          alt_awk_parse: "git branch 2>/dev/null | awk '/^\\*/{printf \"(%s) \", substr($0,3)}'"
        unresolved_contract_questions:
          - detached_head_behavior
          - non_git_repo_behavior
          - git_missing_or_slow_fs_behavior
          - stderr_stdout_discipline
          - branch_name_weird_chars
      - id: notes-capture-prompts
        intent: yac-prompts for high-signal note capture.
        prompts:
          - trigger: what exact annoyance forced the tune?
          - new_behavior: what replaced copy/paste tennis?
          - artifact_path: repo/.hee -> repo/hee -> contracts/ decision points
          - hiera_precedence: concrete override examples
          - footguns: what broke / nearly broke
          - dogfood_proof: what evidence proved it worked
      - id: hee-words-dictionary-and-thesaurus
        intent: YAML-first dictionary of HEE words + optional thesaurus; includes etymology note.
        etymology_note:
          thesis: "Greek θέσις (thésis): a setting down/placing; from τίθημι (tithénai) to put/place"
          thesaurus: "Greek θησαυρός (thēsaurós): treasure/storehouse; indirect cousin link via store/place sense"
      - id: leg1-ideas-to-canon
        intent: formalize how ideas move through system (leg 1 -> canon) with stool+dogfood methodology.
        narrative:
          - oper fatigue triggers tuning using head+keys+sysadmin skills
          - doc starts in repo/.hee
          - moves to repo/hee
          - destined for contracts/ as YAML hee-obj
      - id: yaml-first-foundational-policy
        intent: formalize YAML-first foundational rule + md exception dif; includes migration note for hee/ markdown
      - id: generated-dir-convention
        intent: convention for generated/ as render target for machine friends (docs + jinja outputs).
        evidence:
          cmd: "mkdir generated && git add generated/ && git commit -m 'chore: created generated dir for machine friends'"
          result: "HEE Pre-commit validation passed"

## Idea lifecycle flow (what you just described)
**Trigger:** oper gets tired of copy/paste tennis and uses real sysadmin instincts to tune the system (this is a *feature*, not a deviation).

### Proposed states (progressive hardening)
1) **Scratch / incubation**
   - **`repo/.hee/`**  
   - Purpose: fast iteration, local context, provisional structure.
   - Accepts MD if it’s the “fastest truthful capture,” but is marked as provisional.

2) **Project-level staging**
   - **`repo/hee/`**  
   - Purpose: shared, reviewable, converging structure.
   - Strong preference: YAML-first objects (or “MD with explicit migration intent”).

3) **Canon / governance**
   - **`contracts/`** (and other canonical dirs) as **YAML hee-object**
   - Purpose: authoritative, schema-validated, stable interfaces.

**Key invariant:** movement is always toward **(a) schema validation** + **(b) clear authority** + **(c) deterministic lookup**.

This is the exact “doc started in repo/.hee → moved to repo/hee → destined for contracts/ as YAML hee-obj” path you called out.

---

## Hiera lookup model (lean hard, by design)
We can formalize a **precedence order** (highest wins) that includes:

1) **`system/local/hee`** (machine-local overrides / ops reality)
2) **`home/.hee`** (operator-local overrides / personal workflow)
3) **`repo/.hee`** (repo-local scratch / incubating)
4) **`repo/hee`** (repo-level staging / shared)
5) **`contracts/`** (canon / governance)
6) **schemas / defaults** (if you have formal default objects)

…and we’ll explicitly document:
- what *kinds* of objects are allowed at each tier
- which tiers are permitted to override which keys
- how to detect/flag “authority leaks” (e.g., MD acting as authority when YAML should)

Also: **h/t puppet hiera pain** is a legit provenance note — this is a “we learned the hard way, so we’re doing it consciously” rule.

## Foundational rule to formalize
**Default:** anything intended to be foundational/canonical starts as **YAML (hee-object compliant)**.  
**MD is a render/UX layer**, not the authority.

### Where Markdown *is* correct (reasonable exceptions)
You already named the best example: **human-facing guides** like `gpt-prompting-guide.md`.

So the “dif” we should bake in is basically:

- **YAML-authoritative**: contracts, policies, glossary/dictionary, specs, checklists, workflows, schemas metadata, cards that become canon.
- **MD-correct exception**: documents whose *primary function* is **human reading** (guides, tutorials, narrative explanations), where YAML would be hostile.
  - Even then: we should plan an eventual YAML “authority twin” (or embed the authoritative YAML and render it), *if/when* it becomes truly foundational.

That matches your “it lives under `hee/` so it’s aspiring-to-foundational” warning. ✅

## Concrete formalization outcome
We should end up with something like:

- A **YAML policy object**: “Foundational artifacts are YAML-first”
- A **diff/decision section**: “When MD is correct”
- A **migration note**: “MD in `hee/` is provisional; expected to migrate to YAML authority + MD render later”

…and this should itself be **hee-object compliant**.

## Your `generated/` change
That commit is totally reasonable:

- `mkdir generated`
- `git add generated/`
- `git commit -m 'chore: created generated dir for machine friends'`

Only thing to decide later (in the same policy family): whether `generated/` is:
- committed-but-empty (with a `.gitkeep` or README),
- committed-as-structure + ignored contents,
- or entirely gitignored.

But the action you took is consistent with “make space for machine outputs.” 🤖👍

First recorded in 1350–1400; Middle English, from Latin, from Greek thésis “a setting down, something set down ...Read more","Dictionary.com","Wiktionary",[837],[10458],"Yep — there’s a **real etymological connection**, but it’s *indirect* and easy to overstate. 🙂

## Are **thesis** and **thesaurus** related?
- **Thesis** comes from Greek **θέσις (thésis)** = “a setting down / placing; a proposition,” from the verb **τίθημι (tithénai)** “to put, place.” citeturn0search0turn0search4turn0search6  
- **Thesaurus** comes from Greek **θησαυρός (thēsaurós)** = “treasure, treasury, storehouse,” via Latin *thēsaurus*. citeturn0search15turn0search3turn0search1  

### The link
They’re **not the same word**, but many etymology discussions point out that **thēsaurós** is plausibly *related* to the same “put/place” verb-family (**tithénai**) in the sense of “a place where valuables are put/stored.” That’s a “related via Greek roots” relationship, not “thesaurus comes from thesis.” citeturn0search11turn0search0  

So: **cousins, not siblings**.

Here are cleaner/compressed equivalents (pick based on portability/intent):

### Best modern git (simple + fast)
```sh
printf '(%s) ' "$(git branch --show-current 2>/dev/null)"
```

### Even shorter (no extra printf formatting needed)
```sh
echo "($(git branch --show-current 2>/dev/null)) "
```

### Old-school compatible (if `--show-current` isn’t available)
```sh
printf '(%s) ' "$(git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD 2>/dev/null)"
```

### If you want to keep the “parse git branch output” vibe, but tighter
```sh
git branch 2>/dev/null | awk '/^\*/{printf "(%s) ", substr($0,3)}'
```

> “Each commit is independently meaningful, and I’d be happy to revert/cherry-pick/bisect them individually.”

Now, **costs: squash vs preserve commits** (what you *pay*, what you *get*).

## Preserve commits (no squash)

### ✅ Benefits
- **Bisect works inside the PR** (if you kept commits green-ish).
- **Targeted revert/cherry-pick**: revert just “oops lint config” without nuking the whole PR.
- **Blame stays high-signal**: “why did this line change?” points at a specific intent.
- **Audit trail / evidence**: stepwise correctness story (very HEE-coded).
- **Parallel work survives**: if a PR mixes unrelated changes, you keep seams.

### 💸 Costs
- **History noise** if commits are tiny or “fixup/fmt/wip” style.
- **Reverts get gnarly** if commits are not self-contained (dependencies between commits).
- **Review burden**: more commits to scan; more “why did this move twice?” confusion.
- **Policy friction**: some repos enforce linear history / squash-only for hygiene.

> Key nuance: preserving commits only pays off if you *actually* maintain commit quality (ideally: each commit compiles/tests or is clearly-scoped structural moves).

---

## Squash merge

### ✅ Benefits
- **One atomic change**: easy revert, easy mental model.
- **Clean history** for “mechanical” work (reorder, rename, lint churn).
- **Reduces “commit spam”** when you iterated in public.
- **Simplifies governance**: fewer commits to audit, fewer partial states to worry about.

### 💸 Costs
- **Lose internal causality**: bisect can’t pinpoint which step introduced the regression.
- **Blame gets muddy**: “this giant commit changed everything.”
- **Harder cherry-pick** partial changes later.

---

## Your take: “HEE should preserve every commit”
**Directionally yes**, with one guardrail:

### Preserve commits **by default** *only if they’re “meaningful and separable.”*  
If a PR includes lots of “fix lint / adjust / re-run” style commits, preserving them doesn’t add evidence — it adds fog.

So the operational rule becomes:

- **Default = preserve**
- **Exception = squash** when commits are *not independently meaningful* (noise, churn, or too interdependent)

That maps perfectly onto the quote you flagged.

---

## Squash as a fatigue metric (🔥 good signal)
Agree — “squash rate” can be a **MET** for “oper tired / iterating sloppily / cognitive load rising.”

But I’d track it *with context*, or you’ll false-positive on “good squashes” (pure refactors / mechanical reorder).

### Suggested MET fields (for the card)
- `merge_strategy`: squash|merge|rebase
- `commit_quality`: separable|dependent|noisy (quick subjective tag)
- `reason_squash`: churn|mechanical|policy|fatigue|unknown
- `green_commit_ratio` (if you care): how many commits were green in CI

**Heuristic:**
- Squash + “noisy” + “late session” + “many retries” ⇒ fatigue signal
- Squash + “mechanical reorder” + “clean commits” ⇒ not fatigue, just hygiene

Squash when you just want “result landed” with minimal churn.

Here are the practical cases where **no squash (merge commit or rebase)** is actually worth it:

## Preserve commits when…

### ✅ 1) Each commit is a reusable unit
- “Add tool”
- “Add tests”
- “Fix bug”
- “Doc update”
If someone later `git bisect`s, or wants to cherry-pick just the “tool” without the “docs,” separate commits are gold.

### ✅ 2) You’re treating commits as an auditable narrative
HEE-style work often has:
- “introduce contract”
- “wire validation”
- “tighten strictness”
- “fix edge case”
That sequence is useful *as evidence* of reasoning and guardrails evolving.

### ✅ 3) You want *true* blame granularity
`git blame` is dramatically more useful when “why did this line change?” maps to a focused commit, not a mega-squash.

### ✅ 4) You’re landing a series that might be partially reverted
If one commit introduces a regression and another is unrelated, you can revert the bad one without backing out the whole PR.

### ✅ 5) You need bisectability across the PR
If you intentionally made each commit “builds + tests pass,” preserving commits lets you bisect inside the PR. (This is the big one for “correctness under fire.”)

### ✅ 6) Multi-author / review signaling
If multiple people contributed, preserving commits keeps attribution and review context cleaner.

---

## Squash when…
- It’s mostly **reorder / rename / formatting / cruft cleanup**
- The intermediate commits are messy (“fix lint”, “oops”, “try again”)
- You don’t expect anyone to need partial revert/cherry-pick
- You want “one change, one commit” for traceability

---

## A good heuristic that won’t lie to you
Preserve commits **only if** you can honestly say:

> “Each commit is independently meaningful, and I’d be happy to revert/cherry-pick/bisect them individually.”

If not, squash.

---

## In your specific screenshot context (reorder/clean cruft)
That’s *usually* a squash, **unless** you deliberately staged it as:
1) pure move/rename commit  
2) behavior change commit  
3) policy/CI change commit  

…because those are exactly the kinds of boundaries you might want to revert independently.

### Squash merge (single commit)
```bash
gh pr merge --squash \

  --body $'Reorder and Clean: Complete\
[x]\
' \

```

### Merge commit (preserve all commits + a merge commit)
```bash

  --subject 'ci: green' \
  --body $'Reorder and Clean: Complete\
[x]\
' \
  --delete-branch
```

What you’re seeing in the PR (“`\
---\
`”) is just **shell quoting**: your `--body "...\

## Update PR body (simple, reliable)

### ✅ Best: heredoc into `--body-file -` (no escaping games)
```bash
gh pr edit 136 --body-file - <<'EOF'
Reorder and Clean Cruft
---
EOF
```

(Use your PR number instead of `136` if different.)

### ✅ Also fine: ANSI-C quoting (interprets `\
`)
```bash
gh pr edit 136 --body $'Reorder and Clean Cruft\
---\
'
```

### ✅ Or: edit interactively in your editor
```bash
gh pr edit 136 --body
```
This opens your `$EDITOR` (vim/nano/etc). Save/quit → updates PR body.

---

## Why your command didn’t “just work”
This part:

```bash
--body "Reorder and Clean Cruft\
---\
"
```

In double quotes, `\
` is **not** turned into a newline by default in POSIX shells, so it lands in GitHub as the literal characters `\` and `n`.

---

## Bonus: if you want “current PR” without typing the number
From the branch that owns the PR:
```bash
gh pr edit --body-file - <<'EOF'
Reorder and Clean Cruft
---
EOF
```

That usually works because `gh` infers the PR from the checked-out branch.

So it must be quoted.

Also: `gh pr checks --json … -q '…'` is running a jq filter. Your filter `.state != SUCCESS` makes jq think `SUCCESS` is a function/variable → boom.

### ✅ Fix (show non-success checks)
```bash
gh pr checks --json state,completedAt,description,link,name,workflow \
  -q '.[] | select(.state != "SUCCESS")'
```

### ✅ If you only want the state + name lines
```bash
gh pr checks --json state,name,workflow,link \
  -q '.[] | select(.state != "SUCCESS") | "\(.state)\t\(.workflow)\t\(.name)\t\(.link)"'
```

### ✅ If you want to *fail the command* when anything isn’t SUCCESS
```bash
gh pr checks --json state,name \
  -q '([.[] | select(.state != "SUCCESS")] | length) == 0'
```
- prints `true` if all success, `false` otherwise (exit code still 0 though)
- if you need a non-zero exit, wrap in shell logic:

```bash
gh pr checks --json state,name \
  -q '([.[] | select(.state != "SUCCESS")] | length) == 0' \
| rg -q '^true$' || { echo "checks not all SUCCESS" >&2; false; }
```

# markdownlint-cli2 configuration (docs-heavy / low-churn profile)
# CLI runner: https://github.com/DavidAnson/markdownlint-cli2
# Rules:  https://github.com/DavidAnson/markdownlint/blob/main/doc/Rules.md#rules

config:
  default: false # disable all rules by default

  MD003:
    style: atx
  # MD003 — heading-style
  # Keep headings consistent: prefer ATX style (## Heading).

  MD009: true  # trailing spaces
  MD010: true  # hard tabs
  MD012: true  # multiple blank lines  

  MD013:
    line_length: 160
    code_blocks: false
    tables: false
  # MD013 — line-length
  # Line-length is noisy in docs; enforce only outside docs (see overrides).
  # (If you want a global default anyway, set it here; override will disable in docs.)

  MD022: true  # heading spacing

  MD024:
    siblings_only: true
  # MD024 — no-duplicate-heading
  # Duplicate headings are usually confusing. siblings_only reduces false positives.

  MD025: true
  # MD025 — single-title
  # Only one H1 per document.

  MD029:
    style: one_or_ordered
  # MD029 — ordered-list-item-prefix
  # Ordered list numbering style is mostly preference; tolerant mode reduces noise.

  MD030: true  # list marker spacing

  MD033:
    allowed_elements:
      - br
      - details
      - summary
      - kbd
      - img
  # MD033 — no-inline-html
  # Allow a small set of practical HTML elements commonly used in docs.

  MD036: false
  # MD036 — no-emphasis-as-heading
  # Bold-as-heading is common in docs; disable to avoid churn.

  MD040: true
  # MD040 — fenced-code-language
  # Require language tags on fenced code blocks (```bash, ```yaml, etc.).
  # High-signal: improves readability + highlighting + tooling.

  MD041: true
  # MD041 — first-line-heading
  # File should start with an H1 heading.

  MD060:
    style: padded
  # MD060 — table-column-style
  # Keep table formatting consistent; padded matches common editor output.

overrides:
  # Docs: disable line-length entirely (prose, URLs, templates, history capsules).
  - files:
      - "docs/**"
    config:
      MD013: false

  # Templates: structure rules often intentionally violated.
  - files:
      - "docs/TEMPLATES/**"
    config:
      MD041: false
      MD025: false

### No special URI scheme built into markdownlint
markdownlint doesn’t use a `mdlint://…` or `markdownlint://…` scheme or anything like that. It’s just normal URLs (http/https) in comments, and rule IDs like `MD040` are just identifiers in config.

### But there *is* a consistent URL pattern people use
Rule docs live in the markdownlint repo under **`doc/Rules.md`**, and GitHub supports header anchors. So folks commonly link like:

```text
https://github.com/DavidAnson/markdownlint/blob/main/doc/Rules.md#md040---fenced-code-language
```

and similarly:

```text
https://github.com/DavidAnson/markdownlint/blob/main/doc/Rules.md#md013---line-length
```

So the “scheme” is really just: **GitHub blob URL + anchor to the rule section**.

### Quick way to find the exact anchor
GitHub generates anchors from the header text in `Rules.md`. You can usually guess it:

- `MD040 - Fenced code language` → `#md040---fenced-code-language`
- `MD013 - Line length` → `#md013---line-length`

(Triple dashes happen because GitHub turns punctuation/spaces into hyphen runs.)

### If you want it extra-clean in your config comments
You can replace the repo-level links with the rule doc links:

```yaml
# CLI runner: https://github.com/DavidAnson/markdownlint-cli2
# Rules docs: https://github.com/DavidAnson/markdownlint/blob/main/doc/Rules.md

config:
  # MD040 docs: https://github.com/DavidAnson/markdownlint/blob/main/doc/Rules.md#md040---fenced-code-language
  MD040: true
```

## Markdown link formats

### Normal link
```md
[link text](https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/blob/<ref>/<path>)
```

### Raw link (good for “evidence” / deterministic fetches)
```md
[raw](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/<owner>/<repo>/<ref>/<path>)
```

### Pinned to a commit (best “evidence”)
```md
[raw @ <shortsha>](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/<owner>/<repo>/<sha>/<path>)
```

### Jump to lines in GitHub UI (super handy for reviews)
GitHub supports `#Lx-Ly` anchors on `blob` URLs:

```md
[see lines 12–45](https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/blob/<ref>/<path>#L12-L45)
```

Notes:
- This works on `github.com/.../blob/...`
- It **does not** work on `raw.githubusercontent.com` (raw is just file bytes, no line UI)

---

## GitHub raw URL schemes

### 1) “Raw” host (recommended for tooling)
**Format:**
```
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/<owner>/<repo>/<ref>/<path>
```

- `<ref>` can be a **branch** (`main`), a **tag** (`v1.2.3`), or a **full commit SHA**
- `<path>` is the file path in the repo

**Examples:**
- Branch:
  ```
  https://raw.githubusercontent.com/spencerbutler/market-thesis/main/.github/workflows/ci.yml
  ```
- Commit pin (most deterministic):
  ```
  https://raw.githubusercontent.com/spencerbutler/market-thesis/<SHA>/.github/workflows/ci.yml
  ```

> Note: the `refs/heads/...` segment you used is accepted sometimes, but the clean canonical form is just `<ref>` (e.g., `main`).

---

### 2) “Blob” URL (human view in GitHub UI)
**Format:**
```
https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/blob/<ref>/<path>
```

Example:
```
https://github.com/spencerbutler/market-thesis/blob/main/.github/workflows/ci.yml
```

---

### 3) “Tree” URL (directory listing)
**Format:**
```
https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/tree/<ref>/<path-to-dir>
```

---

### 4) Raw via github.com with a query (less clean)
Sometimes you’ll see:
```
https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/raw/<ref>/<path>
```
It often works, but `raw.githubusercontent.com` is the more standard “direct content” endpoint.

---

## Quick rule of thumb
- **Machines / curl / linters** → use `raw.githubusercontent.com` + **commit SHA** when you want “never changes.”
- **Humans** → use `github.com/.../blob/...`

The value "warning" ...Read more",[],[11466],{"_814":815,"_816":817,"_818":1756},[11468],"In `markdownlint` land, `default` is a **rule tag**, not a magic YAML keyword.

So this:

```yaml
config:
  default: false
```

means:

- **Disable the `default` rule set/tag** → i.e. **turn off *all* rules by default**
- Then you explicitly enable only the rules you list afterward.

That behavior is documented in the `markdownlint` config docs: you can set `"rule_tag_or_default": false` to disable the specified rule/tag/`default`. citeturn0search2

### What it looks like in practice
With:

```yaml
config:
  default: false
  MD040: true
  MD013: false
```

You get:
- ✅ Only `MD040` runs (enabled)
- ❌ `MD013` is explicitly disabled (even if it would’ve been enabled)
- ❌ Everything else stays off because `default: false`

You’ll see this pattern in real repos, too (GitLab uses `default: false` and then whitelists rules). citeturn0search12

— this is mostly about **config discovery** and **naming conventions**, not your PS1 😄

### Should `safe.markdownlint-cli2.yaml` be a dotfile?
If you want `markdownlint-cli2` to **auto-discover** it without flags: **yes**, it needs to be one of the **supported default names**, which are dotfiles like:

- `.markdownlint-cli2.jsonc`
- `.markdownlint-cli2.yaml`
- (also `.markdownlint.jsonc/.json`, `.markdownlint.yaml/.yml`, etc.) citeturn0search0

So `safe.markdownlint-cli2.yaml` **won’t** be picked up automatically by default name search. Making it a dotfile like `.markdownlint-cli2.yaml` is the “it just works” path.

---

## How does `.markdownlint-cli2.yaml` get read?
`markdownlint-cli2` searches for config files by **conventional filenames** (above) in the working directory / relevant scope, and it also supports pointing to a config explicitly via CLI flags. citeturn0search0turn0search1

### Practical patterns
### ✅ Pattern 1: canonical dotfile (recommended)
Keep **one** canonical config:
- `.markdownlint-cli2.yaml` in repo root

Run normally:
```bash
markdownlint-cli2 .
```

### ✅ Pattern 2: “safe profile” file + explicit `--config`
Keep multiple configs:
- `safe.markdownlint-cli2.yaml`
- `strict.markdownlint-cli2.yaml`
…and select one explicitly:

```bash
markdownlint-cli2 --config safe.markdownlint-cli2.yaml .
```

(That’s the clean way to keep “profiles” without fighting discovery.) citeturn0search0turn0search1

### ✅ Pattern 3: directory-specific overrides
If you drop a `.markdownlint-cli2.yaml` inside a subdirectory, tools commonly use that to customize behavior for that directory. citeturn0search2

---

## A nice compromise for “safe.*” without renaming
If you *want* the file to be named `safe.markdownlint-cli2.yaml` but still have automatic discovery, you can:
- keep `.markdownlint-cli2.yaml` as a **thin wrapper** that points to / mirrors the safe file (depending on how you run it)

But simplest is: **dotfile = default**, “safe/strict” = explicit `--config`.

---

## Read repo rulesets from CLI
You can do this two ways:

### 1) GitHub CLI (gh) with REST
List rulesets:
```bash
gh api -H "Accept: application/vnd.github+json" \
  /repos/spencerbutler/market-thesis/rulesets
```

Get one ruleset in detail (replace `<ID>` from the output above):
```bash
gh api -H "Accept: application/vnd.github+json" \
  /repos/spencerbutler/market-thesis/rulesets/<ID>
```

That’ll show the exact required status checks (and whether admin bypass is allowed).

### 2) GraphQL (also via `gh api graphql`)
Useful if you want more structured queries, but REST is easiest here.

---

## Write/edit repo rulesets from CLI?
**Possible**, but not “nice.”

- There isn’t a first-class `gh ruleset edit …` command today.
- You *can* **PATCH** the ruleset via the REST API with `gh api -X PATCH …`, **but** you must send the full/valid ruleset payload (easy to footgun).
- Because of that, for a one-off fix like “required check name is wrong,” the **UI is the safe move**.

---

## If you still want the CLI write path anyway (guardrails: “show me, don’t tell”)
Here’s the workflow I’d use to avoid a footgun:

1) **Fetch** current ruleset JSON to a file:
```bash
RID="$(gh api /repos/spencerbutler/market-thesis/rulesets --jq '.[0].id')"
gh api -H "Accept: application/vnd.github+json" \
  /repos/spencerbutler/market-thesis/rulesets/$RID > /tmp/ruleset.json
```

2) **Inspect** required checks in that JSON:
```bash
rg -n "required_status_checks|status_checks|workflows|ci.yml|integrity" /tmp/ruleset.json
```

3) **Edit** the JSON carefully (this is the dangerous part) and PATCH it back:
```bash
gh api -X PATCH -H "Accept: application/vnd.github+json" \
  /repos/spencerbutler/market-thesis/rulesets/$RID \
  --input /tmp/ruleset.json
```

⚠️ Caveat: this may fail if the returned JSON includes read-only fields or doesn’t match the PATCH schema exactly. You often need to construct a “clean” PATCH body rather than re-uploading the GET response verbatim.

---

### Recommendation for *this* incident
Use CLI to **read** + confirm (great), then use UI to **change the required check** from `.github/workflows/ci.yml` → `integrity`. After that, your merges/pushes will work instantly.

If you want, paste the output of:
```bash
gh api /repos/spencerbutler/market-thesis/rulesets --jq '.[].id'
```
…and I’ll give you a *safe* minimal PATCH payload that only changes the required check field (no full ruleset rewrite).",{},{"_752":11831,"_759":11850,"_54":11851,"_762":11852,"_764":765,"_766":34,"_767":815,"_769":11853,"_771":772},"bd0a0b7c-4e73-48df-b8a9-b95a5fdeb690",[11816],{"_843":1637,"_769":11855},1770753257.2027085,{"_838":839,"_840":11854},{"_1634":34,"_786":11841,"_788":789,"_790":67,"_66":67,"_791":7348,"_793":11848,"_794":11842,"_796":10,"_1635":34,"_797":14},[828],{},{"_752":11848,"_759":11859,"_54":11860,"_762":11861,"_764":765,"_767":768,"_769":11862,"_771":772},"c347fab1-a50b-4969-8012-6001f412f094",[11831],{"_843":1659,"_769":11870},1770753256.102,{"_838":839,"_840":11868},{"_1646":11863,"_1648":11864,"_1650":11865,"_1652":11866,"_786":11841,"_1654":-5,"_794":11842,"_796":10,"_797":14},[],[],[],{"_1655":11867},[],[11869],"and we read or write the repo rules from cli?",{},{"_752":11857,"_759":11874,"_54":11875,"_762":11876,"_764":765,"_766":34,"_767":768,"_769":11877,"_771":772,"_773":774},"9864583b-8472-4b95-a1ba-9b42636ecf8b",[11848],{"_843":844,"_769":11887},1770753034.483981,{"_838":839,"_840":11885},{"_775":11878,"_777":34,"_783":11879,"_778":11880,"_785":67,"_781":11881,"_786":11882,"_788":789,"_790":67,"_66":67,"_791":7348,"_793":11872,"_794":11883,"_796":10,"_797":34},{"_50":834,"_835":11884},[],[],[],"eeb5d1e9-b8dd-4710-9bcb-5cbab4184a97","ea54b613-6d56-403b-a9a5-24ac4ed8d1f0",[837],[11886],"Bingo. This output nails it ✅

- The **real** required check name is **`integrity`** (shown by `gh pr checks 2 … → SUCCESS integrity`)
- The ruleset is (wrongly) requiring a check named **`.github/workflows/ci.yml`**
- That required check will **never** show up, so GitHub blocks pushes/merges forever.

So the fix is **not more git/gh commands** — it’s **fixing the ruleset’s required check name** to match what Actions actually reports.

### What to change (exactly)
Go to the rules link GitHub printed (you already have it):

- Settings → Rules → (ruleset that applies to `main`) → **Required status checks**
  - **Remove**: `.github/workflows/ci.yml`
  - **Add**: `integrity`  
    (and if it wants the full context string, you saw it as `CI/integrity` in the checks list — but the check name itself is `integrity`.)

Once that’s saved, you’ll be unblocked.

---

## After you change the ruleset: CLI to finish cleanly

### 1) Merge PR #2 (now that policy can be satisfied)
```bash
gh pr merge 2 --merge --delete-branch
```

If it still insists on policy timing, use auto:
```bash
gh pr merge 2 --merge --delete-branch --auto
```

### 2) Merge PR #1 as well (same deal)
```bash
gh pr merge 1 --merge --delete-branch
```

### 3) Sync local main
```bash
git checkout main
git pull --ff-only
```

### 4) If you still have your local “ahead 1” commit after pulling (rare, depends on ordering), resolve with:
```bash
git status -sb
git log --oneline --decorate --graph -10
```

…but in the normal case, the merges will fast-forward you and you’re done 🎉

---

### Why “private → public” matters
It’s consistent with how you got here: ruleset required check got configured (or auto-suggested) with the **workflow file path**, and later your actual job/check settled on **`integrity`**. Visibility/settings changes can expose that mismatch, turning it into a hard block.

If you want the extra-hardening move after you’re green: rename the job/check to something unambiguous (e.g., job id `integrity` is already good), and keep the ruleset requiring that exact check.

When a repo is **private**, GitHub can end up with a ruleset that references a required check in a kinda “path-y / stale” way, and when you flip the repo to **public** (or change Actions settings / default workflow permissions), you can land in a state where:

- the ruleset requires a check name that **doesn’t exist anymore**
- Actions runs might have been **disabled/blocked** during/after the visibility change
- and because the required check is “expected,” GitHub blocks both **pushes** and **merges** forever until the ruleset is corrected

So: visibility change isn’t the *root* problem by itself, but it’s a very plausible “how did my ruleset get into this broken state?” explanation.

### What to do next (concrete + minimal)
Run these **two** commands:

```bash
gh pr checks 2
gh run list --limit 20
```

Interpretation:
- If `gh run list` shows **no runs**, Actions likely didn’t run (disabled/permissions). Then go to repo **Settings → Actions → General** and ensure Actions is enabled + “Workflow permissions” allow normal operation.
- If runs exist, `gh pr checks 2` will show the **real check names** (e.g. `CI / <job>`). Then the fix is 100%: update the ruleset required check from `.github/workflows/ci.yml` to the real name.

### Why the current required check is wrong
Rulesets require the **check-run name**, not the workflow filename/path. A required check called `.github/workflows/ci.yml` is basically a “phantom requirement” unless you somehow created a check with that exact literal name (you didn’t).

```bash

```

That’s why:

- direct push to `main` is blocked ✅
- PR merge is blocked ✅
- even `--admin` can’t help if the ruleset is configured to **disallow bypass / require checks always** ✅

So the “fix via CLI” is: **prove what checks actually exist**, then you must **change the required check name in the ruleset** (almost certainly via UI). CLI can’t reliably edit rulesets today.

Here are the exact commands to get the decisive evidence + unblock path.

---

## 1) Prove the checks that actually exist on PR #2
```bash
gh pr checks 2 --json name,state,link --jq '.[] | "\(.name)\t\(.state)\t\(.link)"'
```

Also show the workflow runs:
```bash
gh run list --limit 20
```

And if you want to drill into the latest run:
```bash
gh run view --log-failed
```

What you’re looking for: check names like `CI / <job>` (e.g. `CI / ci`). **You will not see** a check literally named `.github/workflows/ci.yml`.

---

## 2) If CI never ran (possible), force a run and re-check
If Actions didn’t run (or is disabled), trigger it:

```bash
gh workflow list
gh workflow run CI || true
gh run list --limit 10
```

If `gh workflow list` shows your workflow but no runs appear, Actions may be disabled at repo/org level.

---

## 3) The actual unblock: fix the ruleset required check name (UI), then re-run checks
Once you’ve run CI at least once, you’ll know the real check name from step (1). Then:

- Go to: repo → **Settings → Rules → ruleset for `main` → Required status checks**
- Remove the bogus one: **`.github/workflows/ci.yml`**
- Add the real one you saw from `gh pr checks 2` (e.g. **`CI / ci`**)

After changing the ruleset, do:

```bash
gh pr checks 2 --watch
gh pr merge 2 --merge --delete-branch --auto
```

---

## 4) If you want to keep going entirely from CLI after the UI tweak
After merge:

```bash
git checkout main
git pull --ff-only
git push -u origin main
```

(That last push should become a no-op / succeed depending on divergence.)

---

### The only “pure CLI” alternative (if you refuse UI)
Delete/disable the ruleset via API. That’s **possible**, but it’s fiddly (needs the ruleset ID + REST calls + auth scopes) and easy to footgun. Given your goal is “first PR of repo,” the UI tweak is the sane move.

---

## ✅ Route A (best): enable auto-merge, then let policy resolve itself
This tells GitHub: “merge it as soon as required checks pass.”

```bash
gh pr merge 2 --merge --delete-branch --auto
```

Now watch until CI + any other requirements go green:

```bash
gh pr checks 2 --watch
```

If it finishes green, GitHub will merge automatically.

---

## Route B: inspect what policy is blocking (so you can fix the exact requirement)
### 1) See PR status + merge blockers
```bash
gh pr view 2 --json mergeable,mergeStateStatus,statusCheckRollup,reviewDecision --jq '
{
  mergeable: .mergeable,
  mergeStateStatus: .mergeStateStatus,
  reviewDecision: .reviewDecision,
  checks: (.statusCheckRollup[]? | {name: .name, status: .status, conclusion: .conclusion})
}'
```

### 2) Quick human-readable check list
```bash
gh pr checks 2
```

---

## If the required check is STILL the bogus `.github/workflows/ci.yml`
This is the key: GitHub rulesets require the **check run name**, not the workflow file path.

To print the check names that *actually exist* on the PR (so you can match them in rules):
```bash
gh pr checks 2 --json name,state,link --jq '.[] | "\(.name)\t\(.state)\t\(.link)"'
```

If you see names like `CI / <job>` (common), then your ruleset is requiring the wrong thing and will never be satisfied until you update the ruleset.

CLI can’t reliably edit rulesets today, so the fastest fix is UI:
- Settings → Rules → ruleset → Required status checks
- replace `.github/workflows/ci.yml` with the real check name you just printed

Then rerun:
```bash
gh pr checks 2 --watch
gh pr merge 2 --merge --delete-branch --auto
```

---

## If you just want to force it (admin hammer)
Only if you’re okay bypassing the policy:

```bash
gh pr merge 2 --merge --delete-branch --admin
```

---

### What I’d do right now (minimal commands)
```bash
gh pr checks 2
gh pr merge 2 --merge --delete-branch --auto
gh pr checks 2 --watch
```

So the confusing bit isn’t “file missing.” It’s this:

### ✅ You’re in a **ruleset bootstrap deadlock**
GitHub is enforcing: **“Required status check `.github/workflows/ci.yml` must exist before updating `main`.”**

But **status checks are produced by Actions runs**, and Actions runs (for `push` to `main`) only happen **after** the ref update… which GitHub is refusing. So the check can’t be produced *by the very push that is being blocked*.

That’s why you can have the file on `main` and still get:

> Required status check ".github/workflows/ci.yml" is expected.

Also, your local output shows you’re trying to push a commit that **doesn’t touch the workflow**:

- `main...origin/main [ahead 1]` → you have 1 new commit locally, not on GitHub `main`
- last commit is “add .hee to gitignore”
- workflow is tracked, but **not part of the pending update** (it’s already on remote)

So you’re hitting protection *on the branch update itself*, not on workflow existence.

---

## The fix that will work immediately (no guessing): PR path
Do this:

```bash
git checkout -b chore/bootstrap-main
git push -u origin chore/bootstrap-main
```

Open a PR from `chore/bootstrap-main` → `main`.

- The PR will trigger your `pull_request:` workflow.
- CI will run and report *real check names*.
- Then merge the PR (rulesets are designed for this flow).

---

## After CI runs once: fix the ruleset check name
Right now your ruleset is requiring a check named **literally** `.github/workflows/ci.yml`.

That is almost certainly **the wrong check name**.

GitHub usually exposes checks like:
- `CI / <job-name>` (ex: `CI / ci`)
- not the file path.

So after the PR runs, go to the ruleset and set the required check to the **actual reported** check name from the PR’s checks list.

(If you leave it requiring `.github/workflows/ci.yml`, it may *never* be satisfiable.)

---

## One more “wait, why is `origin/…` weird?” note
Your log shows:

- `HEAD -> main, origin/chore/update-gitignore, chore/update-gitignore`

That means you have a remote-tracking ref pointing at your current commit for that branch, but `origin/main` is still behind (since your `main` push was blocked). Not a crisis — just explains the “ahead 1” situation.

",{},{"_752":12129,"_759":12146,"_54":12147,"_762":12148,"_764":765,"_766":34,"_767":768,"_769":12149,"_771":772,"_773":774},"887ce7ca-5d52-4114-a7d6-a541beeae6e0",[12120],{"_843":844,"_769":12159},1770752426.233576,{"_838":839,"_840":12157},{"_775":12150,"_777":34,"_783":12151,"_778":12152,"_785":67,"_781":12153,"_786":12154,"_788":789,"_790":67,"_66":67,"_791":7348,"_793":12144,"_794":12155,"_796":10,"_797":34},{"_50":834,"_835":12156},[],[],[],"2e497641-495c-41c5-8a42-4cff0917823f","5bb4de70-3f82-4538-a3c5-2d014e2f7f4f",[837],[12158],"Ahhh yep — *classic* GitHub gotcha 😄 The file exists **in your working tree**, but GitHub is saying the **required check hasn’t been produced for `main`** yet. That can happen for a few very specific reasons.

Here are the most common causes, in the order I’d bet on them:

## 1) The workflow file isn’t actually on GitHub yet (not committed / not pushed)
Even though it’s on disk locally, if it’s not in the commit you’re pushing, GitHub can’t run it → no check → push rejected.

Run:

```bash
git status -sb
git ls-files .github/workflows/ci.yml
git log -1 --name-status
```

What you want to see:
- `git status` does **not** show `?? .github/workflows/ci.yml` (untracked) or ` M ...` (modified but uncommitted)
- `git ls-files` prints the path (means it’s tracked)
- `git log -1 --name-status` shows it was included in the last commit you’re trying to push

If it’s untracked, do:

```bash
git add .github/workflows/ci.yml
git commit -m "ci: add workflow"
```

…and *then* push.

---

## 2) The required check name in the ruleset doesn’t match what Actions reports
Rulesets require an **exact check name**. The error text showing `.github/workflows/ci.yml` is a hint that the rule might be configured to require the *workflow filename* (or some stale check name), but GitHub checks are usually named like:

- `CI / ci` (workflow name + job name), or
- whatever the workflow/job is named

So the rule may be requiring a check that will **never exist**, even though the workflow file exists.

✅ Fix: run the workflow once (via PR or after a non-protected push), then go to **Settings → Rules → ruleset → Required status checks** and select the *actual* check name that appeared.

---

## 3) “Require status checks before merging” + “no pushes to main” creates a bootstrap deadlock
If your ruleset blocks direct pushes to `main` *and* requires CI checks, then the **first time** you populate the repo you must do it via **PR** (because pushes to main are blocked until checks exist, but checks don’t exist on main until code is there).

Fast escape hatch:

```bash
git checkout -b chore/bootstrap
git push -u origin chore/bootstrap
```

Open PR → CI runs → merge → main becomes legit.

---

## 4) Actions is disabled, or workflow permissions prevent it from running
Less likely, but possible:
- Actions turned off for the repo/org
- Workflow permissions set in a way that blocks runs
- Using a self-hosted runner label that doesn’t exist (would show in the workflow file)

---

# The quickest “no-guessing” triage (2 commands)
Paste the output of these two commands (they’re short and decisive):

```bash
git status -sb
git ls-files --stage .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

### How to interpret
- If `git status` shows the workflow as `??` or ` M`, it’s not in the commit → **#1**
- If `git ls-files --stage` prints nothing, it’s not tracked → **#1**
- If both look good, it’s almost certainly **#2 or #3** (mismatched required check name / bootstrap deadlock)

If you don’t want to paste anything, the safest move that works for **#2 and #3** is: **push a branch and open a PR** (Option 3 above). ### What the error actually means
- Your repo has a rule on `main` that says: **a required status check named `.github/workflows/ci.yml` must report** before updates to `main` are allowed.
- GitHub currently **expects** that check (by name), but it **doesn’t exist / isn’t running / hasn’t reported**, so GitHub rejects the push with **GH013**.

The “Total 0 (delta 0)” bit is just “nothing new to send” at the packfile level; the rule rejection still blocks the ref update.

## Fix options (pick one)

### ✅ Option A (recommended): add the missing workflow so the required check can exist
1. Create this file: `.github/workflows/ci.yml`
2. Commit it
3. Push again

Here’s a tiny starter workflow that always runs on pushes/PRs and reports a check named after the workflow (`CI`) plus job (`ci`). **But** your rule is expecting a check literally keyed to `.github/workflows/ci.yml` (rulesets sometimes show it like that). To be safe, name the workflow/job cleanly and then adjust the ruleset to require the actual check name GitHub reports (see Option B note).

Example minimal workflow:

```yaml
name: CI
on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]
  pull_request:

jobs:
  ci:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: echo "CI ok"
```

Then:

```bash
git add .github/workflows/ci.yml
git commit -m "ci: add basic GitHub Actions workflow"
git push -u origin main
```

### ✅ Option B: change the repo rule so it doesn’t require that check (or requires the right name)
Go to the rules link GitHub printed (repo rulesets), and either:
- remove the required check, **or**
- set the required check to the **exact** check name that appears after your workflow runs (typically `CI / ci`).

This is the fastest if you don’t want CI yet.

### ✅ Option C: push a PR branch (if main is protected) and merge via PR
If your rules also block direct pushes to `main` (common), do:

```bash
git checkout -b chore/boot
git push -u origin chore/boot
```

Then open a PR → CI runs → merge → main updates legally.

---
